The production is as close to perfection as it comes, peaking in sheer hilarity when Hildy’s editor, Walter Burns (Lane), roars onstage to sabotage his star reporter’s plans to escape.

Even if not every element in director Jack O’Brien’s lavishly cast production hits the mark, this deluxe Broadway revival nonetheless is crackling entertainment.

The combination of Mr. Lane’s all-consuming passion for the theater and Walter’s for getting the story makes the endangered profession of print journalism feel, for a flickering moment, like the most vital job on the planet.

Of course, Hecht and MacArthur did not write a one-man play with 19 characters and Lane’s electrification of the last third cannot help make the rest feel like vamping.
So it’s a grievous disappointment to report that this much-anticipated revival is slack and lackluster, a case study in how to get a good play wrong.

Nathan Lane and John Slattery star in a revival of the 1928 comedy about the press. It was an age of tawdry scandals reported in hyperbolic headlines, when politicians colluded with police to keep their malfeasance hush-hush, and guys named Roy were very particular about their gluten intake.
Too bad that this time around it’s also an ensemble comedy that feels like a one-man show.
Director Jack O'Brien has not given them the proper pacing for this frantic 1928 farce of foul-mouthed scandal-sheet scribblers cracking wise and chasing scoops in corrupt Chicago.

Lane has given many memorable performances, in such shows as “The Producers” and the revivals of “Guys and Dolls” and “A Funny Thing Happened on the Way to the Forum,” but his show-saving charge to the rescue of “The Front Page” is as impressive as any of them.
It is surprising how much of a slog this nearly three-hour production can be at times until Lane’s entrance, despite the presence of a battalion of talented character actors.
He plays Walter very broadly but nobody does broad better.
Coherent this production is not, but that hasn't yet (and probably won't) stop it from being the most buzzed-about show of the fall.
Like a shot of adrenaline laced with laughing gas, Lane jolts the lopsided and longwinded 1928 chestnut wide awake.
But, in the current staging, the preceding one hour and 45 minutes is only intermittently rollicking and Lane delivers a much needed jolt with his amazing timing, phrasing, and reactions.
I often found myself admiring the production but unable to enjoy it.
Somehow it’s no longer enough, like it or not, to identify with characters’ flaws.
It feels a bit sleazy to watch this play now, a bit tone-deaf — especially the first act.
O’Brien’s gorgeously etched presentation is as good as it gets.
An uproariously funny Broadway staging that expertly captures the work and the period, thanks to a mighty cast, and director Jack O'Brien's super-smart staging.

His worst moment comes when he swallows the play’s best line.

cn.t: Critics praise Nathan Lane's electrifying performance as editor Walter Burns, though most agree he arrives too late to save this nearly three-hour revival of the dated 1928 newspaper farce. The stellar cast outshines the creaky material.
